meta.titre: Graphs in Chemistry: plotting and reading data from tables

sections.contenu_markdown: In a Douala school laboratory, a student drops marble chips into acid and records the volume of gas every 20 seconds. A column of numbers is hard to interpret, but a graph of the same numbers shows at once when the reaction was fast, when it slowed down and when it stopped. In the GCE O/L you are asked to plot data from a table, draw the correct line, read values from it and explain its shape in terms of chemistry. These skills carry easy marks if you follow a fixed routine.

items: The quantity that you change goes on the horizontal axis and the quantity that you measure goes on the vertical axis.
The rate of a reaction is the change in the amount of a substance divided by the time taken.
The gradient of a line is the change in $y$ divided by the change in $x$.
Pure substances melt and boil at fixed temperatures.

sections.titre: Plotting a graph and reading information from it
sections.contenu_markdown:
A graph turns a table of results into a picture, so that trends can be seen and values read off. Plot the quantity that you **change or control** (time, temperature, volume of acid added) on the **x-axis** and the quantity that you **measure** on the **y-axis**.

**Plotting from a table**

1. Choose a scale so that the points fill more than half of the grid in both directions. Use easy scales such as 1, 2, 5 or 10 squares per unit.
2. Label each axis with the quantity and its unit, for example *Volume of gas (cm$^3$)* and *Time (s)*.
3. Plot every point as a small, neat cross.
4. Draw a **smooth curve** or a **single straight line of best fit** through the points. Do not join the points with short ruler lines, and ignore a point that is clearly out of place.
5. Give the graph a title.

**Reading a graph.** To find a value, draw a line from the axis to the curve and then down or across to the other axis. Reading between plotted points is called interpolation.

**Gradient.** The gradient of a line is $\dfrac{\text{change in } y}{\text{change in } x}$. On a graph of amount of product against time, the gradient is the **rate of reaction**: a steep line means a fast reaction and a horizontal line means that the reaction has stopped.

**Average rate** between two times $= \dfrac{\text{change in volume}}{\text{change in time}}$, for example in $\mathrm{cm^3\ s^{-1}}$.

variantes.quand_utiliser: A gas is collected while a reaction takes place.
variantes.contenu_markdown: The curve is steepest at the start, when the concentration of the reactant is highest. It becomes less steep as the reactants are used up and becomes horizontal when one reactant has all reacted. Compare two experiments on the same graph: a higher concentration, a higher temperature or smaller particles (powder) give a **steeper** curve, but if the amount of the limiting reactant is the same, both curves level off at the **same final volume**.

variantes.quand_utiliser: Temperature is plotted against time for a substance heated or cooled steadily.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Sloping parts show a single state being heated. The **flat parts** show a change of state: at the melting point (solid and liquid together) and at the boiling point (liquid and gas together). The temperature stays constant because the heat supplied is used to overcome the forces between particles, not to speed them up. A pure substance has a sharp melting point, whereas an impure one melts over a range of temperature and at a lower temperature. A cooling curve has a flat part at the freezing point.

variantes.quand_utiliser: Solubility is plotted against temperature, or temperature against volume of acid added.
variantes.contenu_markdown: A solubility curve shows the mass of solute dissolving in 100 g of water at each temperature. The solubility of most solids rises with temperature, so the difference in solubility between two temperatures is the mass that crystallises when a saturated solution cools. In a thermometric titration the temperature rises in a nearly straight line while acid is neutralising the alkali (exothermic), then falls slowly when excess cold acid is added. Draw the two straight lines: where they cross is the **end point** and the volume at that point is the volume of acid needed.

sections.enonce_markdown:
Marble chips (calcium carbonate) were added to an excess of dilute hydrochloric acid and the carbon dioxide produced was collected in a gas syringe. The results are in the table.

| Time (s) | 0 | 20 | 40 | 60 | 80 | 100 | 120 | 140 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Volume of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ (cm$^3$) | 0 | 28 | 46 | 58 | 66 | 70 | 72 | 72 |

(a) Describe how to plot the graph. (b) After how many seconds did the reaction stop? (c) Calculate the average rate of reaction in the first 20 s and between 60 s and 80 s. (d) Explain the change in rate. (e) Calculate the mass of calcium carbonate that reacted. $\mathrm{CaCO_{3}\ +\ 2HCl  \rightarrow  CaCl_{2}\ +\ H_{2}O\ +\ CO_{2}}$; molar volume = 24 dm$^3$; C = 12, O = 16, Ca = 40.

etapes.action: Set up the axes and plot.
etapes.justification: Time is the quantity that is controlled, and the volume is measured.
etapes.resultat_markdown: x-axis: Time (s), 0 to 140 with 10 s per big square. y-axis: Volume of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ (cm$^3$), 0 to 80 with 10 cm$^3$ per big square. Plot eight crosses and draw one smooth curve.

etapes.action: Find when the volume stops changing.
etapes.justification: A horizontal part of the curve means that no more gas is produced.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The volume reaches 72 cm$^3$ at 120 s and stays at 72 cm$^3$, so the reaction stopped at **120 s**.

etapes.justification: Rate depends on the number of effective collisions per second.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The acid is used up and the marble chips get smaller, so the concentration of acid and the surface of marble fall and there are fewer collisions per second.

etapes.action: Calculate the mass of calcium carbonate.
etapes.justification: The acid is in excess, so the final volume of gas is fixed by the amount of calcium carbonate.
etapes.resultat_markdown: $n(\mathrm{CO_2}) = \dfrac{72}{24\,000} = 0.0030\ \mathrm{mol}$. The ratio $\mathrm{CaCO_3 : CO_2}$ is 1 : 1, so $n(\mathrm{CaCO_3}) = 0.0030\ \mathrm{mol}$ and $m = 0.0030 \times 100 = 0.30\ \mathrm{g}$.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The reaction stopped at 120 s, the rate fell from 1.4 to 0.40 $\mathrm{cm^3\ s^{-1}}$ as the reactants were used up, and **0.30 g** of calcium carbonate reacted.

items.erreur_markdown: Joining the plotted points with straight ruler lines from one point to the next.
items.pourquoi_faux: Experimental results contain small errors, and a rate graph changes smoothly.
items.correction_markdown: Draw one smooth curve (or one straight line of best fit) that passes as near as possible to all points.

items.erreur_markdown: Labelling the axes only with words such as *time* and *volume*, or putting the measured quantity on the x-axis.
items.pourquoi_faux: Without units the graph is incomplete, and the controlled quantity belongs on the x-axis.
items.correction_markdown: Write quantity and unit on each axis, for example *Time (s)* on the x-axis and *Volume of gas (cm$^3$)* on the y-axis.

items.erreur_markdown: The steeper curve produced more gas.
items.pourquoi_faux: A steeper curve shows a faster rate, not a larger amount. The final volume depends on the amount of limiting reactant.
items.correction_markdown: Compare the steepness for the rate and the height at which the curve levels off for the total amount of gas.

items.erreur_markdown: The flat part of a heating curve means that no heat is being supplied.
items.pourquoi_faux: The heater continues to supply heat; the energy is used to change the state of the substance.
items.correction_markdown: During melting or boiling, the heat energy overcomes the forces between particles, so the temperature stays constant.

items.enonce_markdown:
A pure solid is heated steadily and its temperature is recorded every 2 minutes.

| Time (min) | 0 | 2 | 4 | 6 | 8 | 10 | 12 | 14 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Temperature (°C) | 30 | 50 | 70 | 80 | 80 | 80 | 100 | 120 |

(a) Which quantity is plotted on the x-axis?

(b) State the melting point of the solid.

(c) What is present in the container at 8 minutes?

(d) Explain why the temperature stays constant from 6 to 10 minutes.

(e) Calculate the average rate of temperature rise in the first 4 minutes.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **Time (min)**, because it is the controlled quantity.

(b) The flat part is at **80 °C**, so this is the melting point.

(c) **A mixture of solid and liquid**, because melting is taking place.

(d) The heat energy supplied is used to overcome the forces between the particles while the solid changes into a liquid, not to increase the temperature.

(e) $\dfrac{70 - 30}{4} = $ **10 °C per minute**.

items.enonce_markdown:
The solubility of a salt, in g per 100 g of water, was measured at different temperatures.

| Temperature (°C) | 10 | 20 | 30 | 40 | 50 | 60 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Solubility (g per 100 g water) | 22 | 30 | 38 | 46 | 54 | 62 |

(a) Describe the shape of the graph that you would draw.

(b) Use the graph to find the solubility at 35 °C.

(c) A saturated solution containing 200 g of water at 60 °C is cooled to 20 °C. Calculate the mass of crystals formed.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) A **straight line** sloping upwards: the solubility rises by 8 g per 100 g of water for every 10 °C rise in temperature.

(b) 35 °C is half-way between 30 °C (38 g) and 40 °C (46 g), so the solubility is **42 g per 100 g of water**.

(c) In 200 g of water: at 60 °C, $2 \times 62 = 124\ \mathrm{g}$ dissolved; at 20 °C, $2 \times 30 = 60\ \mathrm{g}$ can stay dissolved. Crystals formed $= 124 - 60 = $ **64 g**.

items.enonce_markdown:
25 cm$^3$ of sodium hydroxide solution of concentration 0.80 $\mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}$ was placed in a polystyrene cup and hydrochloric acid of unknown concentration was added from a burette. The temperature was recorded after each 5 cm$^3$ of acid.

| Volume of acid added (cm$^3$) | 0 | 5 | 10 | 15 | 20 | 25 | 30 | 35 | 40 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Temperature (°C) | 22.0 | 24.0 | 26.0 | 28.0 | 30.0 | 29.5 | 29.0 | 28.5 | 28.0 |

(a) Describe how to find the volume of acid needed for neutralisation from a graph of these results.

(b) State this volume.

(c) Explain why the temperature rises and why it then falls.

(d) Calculate the concentration of the acid. $\mathrm{NaOH\ +\ HCl  \rightarrow  NaCl\ +\ H_{2}O}$
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Plot temperature (y-axis) against volume of acid (x-axis). Draw one straight line through the points from 0 to 20 cm$^3$ and another straight line through the points from 25 to 40 cm$^3$. Extend both lines until they cross; the volume at the crossing point is the end point.

(b) The lines cross at **20 cm$^3$**, where the temperature is at its maximum, 30.0 °C.

(c) Neutralisation is exothermic, so heat is released and the temperature rises while alkali is still present. After the end point no more heat is produced, and the extra acid added is cooler than the mixture, so the temperature falls.

(d) $n(\mathrm{NaOH}) = 0.80 \times 0.025 = 0.020\ \mathrm{mol}$. The ratio is 1 : 1, so $n(\mathrm{HCl}) = 0.020\ \mathrm{mol}$ in $0.020\ \mathrm{dm^3}$. Concentration $= \dfrac{0.020}{0.020} = $ **1.0 $\mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}$**.

items_markdown: Put the controlled quantity on the x-axis, label both axes with quantity and unit, and choose a scale that fills more than half of the grid.
Plot with small crosses and draw a smooth curve or a single line of best fit; never join the points one by one.
The gradient of a volume-time graph is the rate of reaction: steep means fast and horizontal means finished.
A higher concentration, temperature or surface area gives a steeper curve, but the same final volume if the limiting reactant is unchanged.
Flat parts of a heating curve are changes of state: the energy supplied breaks forces between particles and the temperature stays constant.
In a thermometric titration, the crossing point of the two straight lines gives the end-point volume.
